name: Tamil
signature: Curvy and loopy with flat top-bars on many letters, repeated arches, and no continuous head-line.
combination: A consonant carries an inherent 'a' (க = ka). A vowel sign replaces that vowel (க + ா → கா = kā). The puḷḷi ் — a DOT above the letter — removes the vowel entirely (க் = k). Unlike Devanagari, Tamil does NOT fuse the bare consonant into a conjunct: the dot stays visible and both letters keep their full shape. (A handful of Sanskrit-borrowed ligatures are the exception — க்ஷ kṣa and ஸ்ரீ śrī.)
notes: Used by Tamil in this curriculum. The inventory below covers the greeting and self-introduction vocabulary of Chapters 1–2 and grows from there; it is deliberately not the full 247-character grid. Stroke orders are the common handwriting convention, not a standard — Tamil is taught with regional and school-to-school variation. IMPORTANT for authors: a `strokeOrder` list names the PARTS of a letter in writing order; it does NOT by itself say where the pen lifts. All twenty-four letters in this starter inventory have authored, font-checked pen paths (`DUCTUS` in language-ladder's `strokes.ts`). அ, ஆ, இ, எ, ஒ, ச, ண, and ன each have two pen-down runs with one verified lift; எ keeps its first six movements joined before the separate right upright, ஒ keeps its first two loop movements joined before the separate lower bowl, ஆ continues from its upright into the long-vowel loop, இ joins its outer-left climb to the final arch, ச joins its upper-frame movements before the separate lower-left bowl, and ண and ன join their loop-and-arch bodies to the top bar before the separate right upright. க, ந, ர, ற, ள, and ழ each use three pen-down runs with two verified lifts, while ஊ, த, and ஞ use four runs with three verified lifts. உ, ட, ப, ம, ய, வ, and ல are each a single unbroken stroke even though their parts have separate names. There are no unverified letters in this starter inventory. Component descriptions name the pieces a learner can see in the vendored Noto Sans Tamil face; several letters share a straight top bar and are best learned as a family (ச/க, ண/ன, ந, ர, ற).

letters.notes: The compact curl, crossing lower loops, and large outside arch are seven named movements, not seven separate strokes. The first five stay connected; after one lift, the outside climb flows straight into the final arch as the second pen-down run.

letters.notes: Independent short u is the standalone vowel used at the beginning of a syllable. Frame 16 keeps its spiral, outer descent, and long baseline in one pen-down run; the dependent short-u sign ு is a separate mark added to a consonant.

components: the three-run ள form written over its baseline

without lifting, carry the long baseline straight to the right — then lift once

without lifting, turn inward through the loop
without lifting, descend around its inner curl — then lift a second time
set the pen at the bottom of the adjoining upright and draw upward
without lifting, carry the top bar to the right — then lift a third time
set the pen at the top of the separate right upright and draw straight down
letters.strokeOrderNote: four strokes — first write the three joined movements of உ, then add ள in its familiar three-run order (joined movements 1–3, joined 4–5, and separate 6); cited to Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Module 17 with Appendix I Frames 17, 16, and 12

The resulting four-run learner order is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil ஊ outline; Tamil handwriting varies by school.

letters.notes: Independent long ū opens words such as ஊர் (ūr, native place) and ஊசி (ūsi, needle). The manual teaches the letter compositionally: write short உ first, then overlay the already learned ள form.

letters.notes: Independent short e is the second row of Appendix I Frame 5. Its numbered movements stay connected from the left climb through the spiral and lower foot; only the right upright begins after a lift. The dependent short-e sign ெ is a different learner row written before a consonant.

letters.notes: Tamil does not write separate letters for k / g / h — க covers them all, and position in the word decides which you say. Its six numbered movements form three pen-down runs, not six strokes: the upper frame, the lower-left bowl, and the lower-right bowl.

letters.notes: Nga is the nasal partner of க: it supplies the ṅ sound in clusters such as ங்க. Frame 2's two pen-down runs survive the font fit even though the detached upright moves from the handwritten model's left edge to Noto Sans Tamil's right edge.

letters.notes: Ca is the simpler sibling of க: both begin with the same upper frame, but ச keeps only the rounded lower-left bowl and lets the middle bar project to the right. a broad outer bowl returning up the left

without lifting, return up the outer-left side and finish below the top bar

letters.notes: Ña is the palatal nasal heard in combinations such as ஞ்ச. Frame 8's eight numbered movements resolve into four pen-down runs in this font fit: inner loop, top bar, central shoulder-and-descent, and outer bowl.

strokeOrder: start at the top left and draw the left upright straight down to the baseline

letters.notes: The three-sided pa shape is the opening portion of ம: descend the left, cross the bottom, and rise on the right, stopping before ma's added top arch and middle descent.

components: a long horizontal foot to the right

letters.notes: The retroflex stop begins as ṭ and voices to ḍ between vowels. Its spare L-shaped outline is written as one cornering motion: down first, then right, with no lift at the turn.

letters.notes: Dental ta is assembled in four short runs: upper frame, broad right bowl, compact left loop, then the separate low tail. The numbered source order begins by climbing the left upright rather than descending it.

letters.notes: The upright is on the left and the curve on the right — the reverse of what a learner coming from Devanagari tends to assume. The whole letter is ONE motion: the five movements above are parts of a single pen-down run, not five strokes, so the hand does not leave the paper until the last one ends.

letters.notes: One of the plainer shapes, and a reasonable first letter to draw. Frame 9's five numbered movements are parts of one continuous spiral-to-upright motion, not five strokes: the pen stays down until the right upright ends.

without lifting, carry the top bar to the right edge — then lift once

letters.notes: The RETROFLEX n — tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth. Learn it beside ன: ண is ன WITH ONE EXTRA ARCH. Frame 13's adjacent row numbers seven movements, not seven strokes: its first six stay connected through the left spiral, two inner arches, and top bar; only the separate right upright requires a lift. Tamil writes three n-sounds with three letters (ந, ன, ண).

without lifting, draw the middle upright straight down — then lift a second time

letters.notes: The retroflex lateral, made with the tongue tip curled back toward the hard palate. Frame 12's six numbered movements are three strokes, not six: movements 1–3 stay joined through the left loop and descent, movements 4–5 join the middle rise to the top bar, and movement 6 is the separate right upright.

components: a tall left upright joined to a low crossbar
an inner upright and broad right bowl
a detached lower hook and short exit
strokeOrder: start at the lower left and climb the tall upright
without lifting, retrace down the same upright
without lifting, carry the low crossbar to the right — then lift once
set the pen at the upper right and retrace left into the inner upright
without lifting, descend and sweep around the broad right bowl — then lift a second time
set the pen below the body and turn through the detached lower hook — and only now lift
letters.strokeOrderNote: three strokes — three joined left-body and top-bar movements, one lift, two joined inner-upright and right-bowl movements, a second lift, then the detached lower hook; cited to Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I, Frame 7, ழ

strokeOrderSource.citation: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 7, ழ (University of Texas at Austin), p. 193
strokeOrderSource.variation: Appendix I Frame 7 numbers six movements in three pen-down runs: joined movements 1–3 form the left body and bar, joined movements 4–5 retrace into the inner upright and broad right bowl, and separate movement 6 forms the detached lower hook. The bundled Noto Sans Tamil print face simplifies the source's looped left body and high bar into a retraced upright with a low crossbar; the authored path preserves the source's run grouping while fitting that printed outline. Tamil handwriting varies by school; this is one attested three-run order.

letters.notes: The famously Tamil retroflex approximant, often transliterated ḻ. Frame 7's six numbered movements are three strokes rather than six: movements 1–3 stay joined through the left body and bar, movements 4–5 stay joined through the inner upright and right bowl, and movement 6 is the detached lower hook.

components: two arches side by side, giving three legs down to the baseline
the right leg continues BELOW the baseline, sweeps left, and drops into a long descender
strokeOrder: start at the lower left, climb the left side, and arch to the middle
without lifting, descend the first middle upright — then lift once
set the pen at the adjacent middle upright and descend — then lift a second time
set the pen at the middle top, arch over, and descend the right side
without lifting again, sweep left below the baseline and drop into the long descender — and only now lift
letters.strokeOrderNote: three strokes — two joined movements, one pen lift, the adjacent middle descent, a second lift, then two joined movements; cited to Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Frame 10, ற

strokeOrderSource.citation: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 10, ற (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 194
strokeOrderSource.variation: Tamil handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation; there is no single national stroke-order standard. This is one attested order.

letters.notes: The hard/trilled r, distinct from ர. Frame 10's five numbered movements form three pen-down runs: movements 1–2 join, movement 3 restarts on the neighboring middle descent, and movements 4–5 join the right arch to the sweep and descender. In நன்றி the pair ன் + ற is said as a single cluster.

marks.attachesAs: a DOT written above the letter, removing the inherent vowel; unlike Devanagari's virama it does not trigger a conjunct — both letters keep their full shape and the dot stays visible
a vertical stroke with a small top hook, written after the consonant
a hook written above and to the right of the consonant
a dependent long-i sign that joins to or shifts beside the consonant carrier
compositionOrder: write the Tamil consonant carrier first
add the ī vowel sign to replace its inherent vowel

compositionSource.citation: The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0, §12.6.3 Tamil Ligatures, Ligatures with Vowel i and Figure 12-21: U+0BC0 TAMIL VOWEL SIGN II forms consonant-vowel ligatures; ட + ீ → டீ and ல + ீ → லீ (2025)
compositionSource.variation: Unicode verifies encoded carrier-first composition and shows that the ii sign can change shape or position to join cursively with its consonant. This is not a universal handwriting direction, and the source supports no standalone ductus claim or pen-lift count.

marks.attachesAs: a dependent vowel sign that normally ligates with the consonant carrier
compositionOrder: write the Tamil consonant carrier first
add the u vowel sign to replace its inherent vowel

compositionSource.citation: The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0, §12.6.3 Tamil Ligatures, Ligatures with Vowel u and Table 12-28: U+0BC1 TAMIL VOWEL SIGN U normally ligates with its consonant; க + ு → கு (2025)
compositionSource.variation: Unicode specifies encoded carrier-first composition and rendering that normally ligates; this is not a universal handwriting direction, and the source supports no standalone ductus claim or pen-lift count.

marks.attachesAs: a dependent long-u sign that normally ligates with the consonant carrier
compositionOrder: write the Tamil consonant carrier first
add the ū vowel sign to replace its inherent vowel

compositionSource.citation: The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0, §12.6.3 Tamil Ligatures, Ligatures with Vowel u and Table 12-28: U+0BC2 TAMIL VOWEL SIGN UU normally ligates with its consonant; க + ூ → கூ (2025)
compositionSource.variation: Unicode specifies encoded carrier-first composition and rendering that normally ligates; this is not a universal handwriting direction, and the source supports no standalone ductus claim or pen-lift count.

marks.attachesAs: a dependent short-e sign written before and to the left of the primary consonant, though pronounced after it
compositionOrder: in handwriting, write the e vowel sign to the left before the primary consonant
write the Tamil consonant carrier after it; read the result as consonant plus e

compositionSource.citation: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Module 6, Frame 6: the secondary symbol for short e is always placed before the primary letter (University of Texas at Austin, 2009)
compositionSource.variation: Module 6 verifies the handwritten sign-before-carrier order and the sign's left-side placement. It does not supply a standalone directional path or pen-lift count, so no ductus is inferred.

marks.attachesAs: a dependent long-e sign written before and to the left of the primary consonant, though pronounced after it
compositionOrder: in handwriting, write the ē vowel sign to the left before the primary consonant
write the Tamil consonant carrier after it; read the result as consonant plus ē

compositionSource.citation: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Module 7, Frame 7: the secondary symbol for ē is written before the primary consonant (University of Texas at Austin, 2009)
compositionSource.variation: Module 7 verifies the handwritten sign-before-carrier order and the sign's left-side placement. It does not supply a standalone directional path or pen-lift count, so no ductus is inferred.

marks.attachesAs: a double hook written BEFORE (to the left of) the consonant, though pronounced after it
